description: Buscamos llegar a la nominación global construyendo una herramienta de apoyo a la toma de decisiones con sólido respaldo científico, que respete el conocimiento agrícola local aprovechando los datos espaciales. Contamos con una ruta de trabajo clara, validación técnica y un ambiente totalmente colaborativo.
summary: AgroCycle is our answer to the Field Shift challenge: a mobile app that helps farmers decide which crop should follow the current one in their field. A farmer creates an account, marks the field on a map, and records its location, area and main crop. The app brings NASA POWER climate data for that location, analyzes the field and proposes a crop rotation, showing for each crop a score, its expected benefits for soil and resilience, and the risks that need attention. Built by Sowing Star, a multidisciplinary team from Yucatan, Mexico, AgroCycle is designed to support, not replace, farmer judgment and local agronomic expertise.
details:
Across the world, farmers plan each season facing shifting temperatures, unpredictable rainfall and soils that are slowly losing their health, and choosing what to plant after the current crop is rarely simple. AgroCycle was born in Yucatan, Mexico, as our answer to the Field Shift challenge: a mobile app that turns NASA Earth observations into a clear suggestion for the next step in a rotation. A farmer creates an account and allows the app to use their location, which brings a first view of environmental conditions for that place: average temperature, precipitation and soil moisture, drawn from NASA POWER agroclimatology data (MERRA-2). Then the farmer registers a field by placing a pin on a map, which fills in the coordinates, and adds its state, municipality, area in hectares and main crop. In our demonstration, a 600-hectare sorghum field in Caucel, Yucatan.

When the farmer asks for an analysis, AgroCycle evaluates the field and proposes a sequence of crops for the rotation, with an overall score. For each crop it explains the benefits and the risks. In the demo, sorghum is valued for its resistance to high temperatures and temporary drought, with the risk of soil depletion if it is grown continuously, and it is followed by beans, a nitrogen-fixing legume that improves soil fertility and structure, with the caution that it needs a rainfall window or initial irrigation. The goal is to make the reasoning visible, so a farmer or an agronomist can agree, question or adjust it.

We built AgroCycle with humility about what satellites can and cannot say. NASA POWER is a reanalysis and not a weather station in the farmer's field, and the scores are guidance, not yield predictions or a replacement for local expertise. Our design continues with more NASA layers: SMAP for soil moisture, GPM IMERG for rainfall, MODIS vegetation indices to detect when fields are usually bare, ECOSTRESS for evapotranspiration and heat stress, and SRTM terrain to flag slopes prone to erosion. These are planned and are not part of the current demo.

The prototype is a React Native mobile app running on Expo, which uses Google Maps to locate fields and NASA POWER for climate data; our video and slides were made in Canva. AgroCycle is built by Sowing Star, a multidisciplinary team from Yucatan, Mexico: Paola Carolina Astudillo González, Gabriel Ellian Cuevas Huchin, Gael Alexander Hernandez Ek, María José Puerto Angulo and Mario Maximiliano Vallarta Inda.
